title: Sessionwise expert affinity probe — Llama/Mistral/Qwen
content:
Summary:
This note summarizes a focused microbenchmark and tracing exercise to investigate sessionwise expert affinity and its contribution to p95/p99 latency variance across three model families (Llama-derivative, Mistral variants, Qwen). The primary goal was to isolate whether persistent per-session routing decisions (affinity) create hot experts that produce tail latency under mixed-length, long-context workloads and to propose low-risk mitigations for the serving runtime.

Background / motivation:
- Production traces showed recurring tail latency spikes tied to a subset of request sessions that had long-lived context (>8k tokens) and skewed gating patterns.
- Hypothesis: when gating decisions are sticky within a session, a small set of experts become hot, leading to queueing on those expert shards (GPU/stream contention, memcpy stalls, and kernel serialization).
- A secondary concern: long KV-cache lifetime increases resident memory pressure and causes eviction/activity that interacts with expert scheduling.

Environment & baseline:
- Runtime: redwood-serving v0.98-stable (kernel scheduling + routing v2).
- Hardware: 4x A100 80GB (NVLink mesh), 1x host CPU per node, 2 nodes used (expert shards pinned across nodes to exaggerate cross-node serialization).
- Models tested: llama-13b-v2 (MoE partition, 64 experts), mistral-7b-moe (config: 32 experts), qwen-7b-moe (48 experts). All compiled with optimized attention kernels and bf16.
- Workloads: mix of short (<=128 tokens), medium (512-1024), and long-session traces (8k-32k). 60% short, 20% medium, 20% long by request count; but long sessions produce ~60% of tokens.
- Batches: steady-state concurrent sessions = 120, microbatch target = 8, request routing top_k=2.

Experiment design:
1) Session stickiness probe: replay production routing decisions but randomize session-to-session gating initial seeds to compare sticky vs. jittered gating patterns.
2) Affinity heatmap: instrument router to emit per-session expert selection histogram sampled every 10s; combine with per-GPU event counters (queue depth, kernel latency).
3) Controlled synthetic: create contrived sessions that prefer a single expert 80% of the time vs. uniform distribution.
4) Long-context stress: force KV-cache retention and artificially inflate sequence lengths to observe memory-driven effects.

Key tracer outputs (selected):
- router_dispatch_wait: mean 0.9ms, p95 6.4ms, p99 18.9ms (sticky gating)
- expert_exec_kernel: mean 2.3ms, p95 10.2ms, p99 36.7ms (hot expert shards)
- memcpy_h2d (expert payloads): mean 0.6ms, p95 4.7ms (increased for cross-node shards)
- ipc_barrier_wait (expert sync across NVLink): median 0.12ms but spikes aligned with p99 expert_exec_kernel events
- gpu_util (hot shards): 95% sustained but kernel queuing observed (stream queue depth spikes)

Observations:
- Sticky routing increases long-tail latency: comparing sticky vs. jittered gating, p99 latency for end-to-end token generation increased by ~2.8x for long sessions on Llama and Qwen models, ~1.9x on Mistral.
- Hot experts show clear queuing signatures: per-expert queue depth correlates strongly (r=0.78) with end-to-end token p99.
- Cross-node expert placements exacerbate latency: when shards for the same expert span nodes, memcpy and IPC barrier spikes align with long-tail events.
- KV-cache pressure amplifies serialization: large contexts increase resident memory and occasionally trigger minor eviction/compaction cycles that increase memcpy_h2d variance and prolong kernel start latency.
- Mistral's routing gating distribution was slightly more uniform (lower skew) at equivalent top_k, which matches lower p99 increase. Architecture-level differences matter: gating softmax temperature and gating head parameterization influenced skew.

Concrete examples from traces (session A):
- 2026-02-12T14:22:31Z session-A request 142
  - routing: experts [17,17,3,17,17] for 5 consecutive tokens
  - observed: expert 17 queue depth jump from 1->16 within 45ms window
  - effect: request token p99 at that point = 41ms vs baseline 12ms

Hypotheses (root causes):
1) Session-local stickiness causes certain experts to receive bursty sequential traffic beyond per-expert parallelism budget.
2) Cross-node expert shards add non-negligible memcpy and synchronization overhead that converts small queuing into substantial tail latency.
3) KV-cache long-lived contexts increase memory bus contention and occasionally force background compaction that delays kernel launches.
4) Some model gating parameterizations (temperature, head count) produce higher skew; differences across model families explain numeric divergences.

Mitigations tested (and results):
- Gating jitter (per-session epsilon): add a small randomized perturbation to gating logits per token (epsilon sampled from N(0, 0.03)). Result: p99 reduced by ~35% for sticky-heavy scenarios; negligible impact on quality in our generation evals.
- Soft-Auto-sharding: prefer placing the most-used experts on nodes with spare memory/compute in the current window (reactive). Result: reduced cross-node memcpy_h2d p95 by ~45% and p99 token latency by ~22% in runs where placement reacted within 10s.
- Microbatch smoothing: enforce per-expert microbatch cap and spill to idle GPUs (when available) instead of serializing on same stream. Result: throughput drop of ~4% but p99 improved 28%.
- Routing fallback: when per-expert queue depth exceeds threshold (8), route additional tokens to the next-best expert (soft fallback). Result: eliminated extreme spikes but introduced minor incoherence in extremely specialized prompts; acceptable tradeoff for many production workloads.

Operational recommendations (short-term):
1) Enable gating jitter by default for long-context session windows >2k tokens (config flag: routing.session_jitter=on).
2) Implement per-expert queue depth metrics and alerting (Grafana + tracer export). Thresholds: p95 queue depth >6 triggers investigation.
3) Add a lightweight placement advisor that prefers full-expert colocation where it reduces cross-node memcpy (best-effort during scale-up).
4) For customers with strict quality constraints, gate gating-jitter as opt-in via model-variant or rollout policy.

Longer-term architectural items (research/eng):
- Explore explicit per-session routing budgets (bound how many tokens can hit the same expert in window X) with bounded fallback policies to preserve quality.
- Evaluate hybrid gating that mixes deterministic hashing with learned gating to reduce extreme skew while keeping model capacity.
- Investigate kernel-level preemption / multi-stream expert execution to reduce serialization on hot experts.
- KV cache compaction telemetry: instrument and correlate compaction events with kernel start latency; consider opportunistic lazy compaction.

Open questions / next steps:
- Quantify quality impact of gating jitter across a wider eval set (few-shot instruction prompts, code generation, retrieval-augmented sessions). Owner: Ethan Li, due 2026-03-10.
- Implement and stage the per-expert queue depth metrics + alerting. Owner: Soraya Khan, PR #1287 (linked).
- Run a 48h canary rolling gating jitter to measure downstream customer visible regressions. Owner: Marina Duarte.

Notes / references:
- Short reproducibility steps are in github PR linked above (serving-runtime/experiments/session-affinity).
- Dashboard panels: expert-affinity-heatmap, per-expert-queue-depth, p99-by-session-length (grafana link in metadata).

Appendix: quick checklist for engineers reproducing locally:
- Checkout branch: serving-runtime/affinity-probe (PR 1287).
- Use run config: runs/affinity_probe/4xA100.yaml.
- Start tracer with --sample-interval-ms=10 and enable router debug sampling at 5% to collect per-session histograms.
- Synthetic seed files available: experiments/affinity_probe/seeds/*.json (session preference patterns).

End of note.
